The Story of Abhayaghosh Muni

I bow to Lord Jinendra, worshipped with devotion by the gods, and I write the story of Abhayaghosh Muni.

Abhayaghosh was king of Kakandi. His queen was Abhayamati. They loved each other deeply.

One day, Abhayaghosh was wandering in the forest. At that time, a fisherman was carrying a large, live turtle with all four legs tied, hanging from a stick. The sinful king's eye fell upon it. In his foolishness, he drew his sword and cut off all four of the turtle's legs. It is a great tragedy that sinful people mercilessly kill such innocent creatures without any thought of right or wrong! The turtle died on the spot, writhing in agony. Through the merit of dying without food (akam-nirjara), he was reborn as the son of that very king Abhayaghosh, named Chandveg.

One day, the king witnessed a lunar eclipse and became detached. He thought: "If even a great, radiant celestial body like the moon — whose equal cannot be found, who is counted among the gods — can be eclipsed and overcome by another, then what to say of humans, over whom death always hovers? Alas, I am a great fool who has been trapped in sensual pleasures and has never turned my attention to my own welfare. The thick darkness of delusion has blinded both my eyes so that I cannot see the path of my own welfare or walk upon it with care. Caught in this sinful web of delusion, I have turned away from Jain dharma and committed many sins. Alas, how shall I now cross this fathomless ocean of existence and reach the blissful shore? O Lord, grant me the strength to attain the true happiness of the soul."

After this reflection, he resolved: "What has been done is done. Still, I have much time for my duty. Just as I have enjoyed sensual pleasures while living in the world, satisfying my body and senses, so now I should practise the harshest austerities for my soul's welfare and destroy these soul-enemies, the karmas, pursued since beginningless time. This is the complete atonement for my past deeds, and only thus shall I touch the happiness of the crest-jewel." With this firm resolve, Abhayaghosh handed all royal duties to his son Chandveg and took Jain initiation, which is the destroyer of the senses' allurements.

As a monk, Abhayaghosh practised intense austerities with unwavering determination. He endured hunger, thirst, heat, cold, and all manner of hardships with perfect equanimity. His son Chandveg, who was the turtle reborn, grew up to be a powerful king. Though he loved his father, he was also drawn to worldly pleasures and did not follow the path of dharma.

One day, Chandveg went hunting in the forest where his father was meditating. Not recognising the monk as his own father, and seeing him as an obstacle to his hunt, he became angry and ordered his men to harm him. But Abhayaghosh remained unmoved, absorbed in meditation. Seeing the monk's perfect peace, Chandveg's heart was transformed. He realised his mistake and bowed to the monk, asking forgiveness.

Abhayaghosh blessed him and continued his meditation. Through dedicated spiritual practice, he destroyed his karmas and ultimately attained liberation.

This story teaches that even the most sinful can attain liberation through sincere repentance and dedicated practice. King Abhayaghosh committed a terrible act of cruelty, but through his recognition of the impermanence of worldly life and his intense spiritual practice, he rose above his past and attained the highest goal. The wise should never despair of redemption.
